subject: polsci
book: Indian Constitution at Work; Political Theory (NCERT, rationalised)

sections.name: 1.1 Why do we need a Constitution?

concepts.text: A constitution as a set of basic rules that lets members of a society coordinate and trust each other
Coordination and assurance: everyone knows the minimum rules others must follow
Function 1: specifying who has the power to make decisions (allocation of decision-making power)
Function 2: setting limits on government power, e.g. fundamental rights the state cannot violate
Function 3: enabling government to fulfil the aspirations and goals of society (e.g. ending caste discrimination, social justice)
Function 4: expressing the fundamental identity of a people as a political community
Constitutions differ in how they balance national identity with other identities (religion, region, language)
Activity type: thought experiment on a society without agreed basic rules
Meaning of 'constitution' as a written document vs a working body of rules
Mode of promulgation: who wrote the constitution and how much legitimacy they had
Constitutions drafted by popularly backed assemblies carry more authority than those imposed by rulers
Substantive provisions: a constitution must give everyone a reason to accept it (rights, fairness)
Balanced institutional design: separation of powers and checks so no single body can dominate
Balance between rigidity and flexibility: core values protected but amendable to change
Examples of failed constitutions (e.g. post-colonial states whose constitutions were set aside)

sections.name: 1.3 How was the Indian Constitution made?

concepts.text: Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946; re-assembled as Assembly of divided India on 14 August 1947
Composition: members elected indirectly by provincial legislatures under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)
Seat allocation by population (roughly one seat per million), shares for provinces and princely states, and for Muslims, Sikhs and General categories
Representation of diverse groups; dominance of Congress yet inclusion of varied opinions
Procedures: discussion and deliberation, consensus-seeking, open public reasoning
Committees of the Assembly; Drafting Committee chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar
Time taken: about 2 years 11 months; adopted 26 November 1949, came into force 26 January 1950
Inheritance of the nationalist movement: Objectives Resolution (Nehru, 1946) and its principles
Earlier demands: Motilal Nehru Report (1928), Karachi Resolution (1931) on rights
Institutional arrangements: balancing legislature, executive, judiciary and Centre-States
Role of the Government of India Act 1935 in shaping institutional structure

sections.name: 1.4 Provisions adapted from Constitutions of different countries

concepts.text: British: first-past-the-post, parliamentary government, rule of law, Speaker, law-making procedure
United States: charter of fundamental rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary
Irish: Directive Principles of State Policy
French: principles of liberty, equality and fraternity
Canadian: quasi-federal form with strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre
Borrowing was adaptation to Indian conditions, not blind copying
The Constitution as an embodiment of democratic values and a living framework
Exercise type: identify which function of a constitution a given provision serves
Exercise type: true/false on the Constituent Assembly's composition and working
Exercise type: explain why the Indian Constitution has authority (promulgation, substance, design)
Exercise type: match provisions with the countries they were borrowed from

chapters.title: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution

concepts.text: Rights as guarantees that protect individuals from the state and others
Bill of Rights: list of rights written into a constitution and protected from violation
Remedies for violation of rights as the essential feature of a bill of rights
Origins of rights demands in the freedom struggle (Nehru Report 1928)

sections.name: 2.2 Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution

concepts.text: Fundamental Rights vs ordinary legal rights: FR can be changed only by constitutional amendment
FR are not absolute: reasonable restrictions by the state
Right to Equality (Art. 14-18): equality before law, equal protection, no discrimination, equal opportunity in public employment, abolition of untouchability and titles
Right to Freedom (Art. 19-22): six freedoms incl. speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession
Right to life and personal liberty (Art. 21) and its wide judicial interpretation (shelter, livelihood, etc.)
Rights of the accused: protection against arbitrary arrest, right to be told grounds, produced before magistrate within 24 hours, no self-incrimination, no double jeopardy
Preventive detention: meaning and safeguards; criticism of misuse
Right against Exploitation (Art. 23-24): ban on human trafficking, forced labour (begar), child labour in hazardous work
Right to Freedom of Religion (Art. 25-28): freedom of conscience, profess, practise, propagate; equality of all religions; secular state
Cultural and Educational Rights (Art. 29-30): minorities' right to conserve culture and run educational institutions
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32): Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution
Writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto - meaning of each
National Human Rights Commission: role in inquiring into rights violations
Right to Property: removed as a fundamental right by the 44th Amendment (1978), now a legal right
DPSP as non-justiciable guidelines for the state to build a just society
Goals in DPSP: welfare of people, social and economic justice, raising living standards, world peace
Policies: uniform civil code, prohibition of liquor, cottage industries, prevention of cow slaughter, village panchayats
Non-justiciable rights: adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, right to work, free education
Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A) added by 42nd Amendment (1976); list of duties and their status
Examples of DPSP implemented through laws (e.g. RTE, panchayats, MGNREGA-type schemes)

sections.name: 2.4 Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

concepts.text: FR protect individuals and restrain state; DPSP direct the state to act positively
Conflict between FR (right to property) and DPSP (land reform, abolition of zamindari)
Judicial view of harmony: FR and DPSP complement each other
Exercise type: classify situations as violation of which fundamental right
Exercise type: distinguish FR and DPSP; match writs with situations
Direct democracy (citizens decide) vs indirect/representative democracy (citizens elect representatives)
Why elections are needed in large modern societies
Constitution decides rules of elections: who votes, who contests, who supervises, how votes are counted
First Past the Post (FPTP): candidate with the most votes wins, even without majority
Single-member territorial constituencies; plurality system
FPTP can give a party many more seats than its vote share (e.g. Congress in 1984)
Proportional Representation (PR): seats in proportion to vote share
List system of PR: Israel and the Netherlands examples, whole country as one constituency
Single Transferable Vote (STV) used for Rajya Sabha and indirect elections like the President's
Comparison table of FPTP vs PR: constituency size, voter choice, seat-vote proportion, stability
Why India adopted FPTP: simplicity for voters, clear choice of candidate, stable government
FPTP encourages social coalitions within parties and two-alliance competition
Numerical/activity type: compute seat shares under FPTP vs PR from vote data
Reserved constituencies for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Lok Sabha and Assemblies
Only SC/ST candidates contest in reserved seats but all voters of the constituency vote
Delimitation Commission decides which constituencies are reserved
Debate about women's reservation; the Women's Reservation Act 2023 (33%)
Universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18+ can vote (lowered from 21 in 1989)
Right to contest: minimum age 25 for Lok Sabha/Assembly; no educational qualification
Independent Election Commission (Art. 324): superintendence, direction and control of elections
Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners; multi-member body since 1993
Security of tenure of CEC: removal like a Supreme Court judge
Functions: voter rolls, schedule, model code of conduct, ordering re-poll, party recognition, symbols
State Election Commissions conduct local body elections
Role of EVMs and voter turnout trends in Indian elections
Suggested reforms: shift to PR or mixed system, one-third seats for women
Controlling money power: state funding of elections, transparency in expenses
Barring candidates with criminal cases; mandatory disclosure of assets and criminal records
Ban on caste and religion appeals in campaigns; regulating party functioning
Exercise type: identify which reform addresses a given electoral problem
Exercise type: case study on FPTP outcomes and reserved constituencies
Executive as the organ that implements laws and policies
Political executive (elected, changes with elections) vs permanent executive (civil servants)
Presidential system: President is head of state and government, directly elected (USA)
Parliamentary system: PM and cabinet responsible to legislature, nominal head of state (UK, India, Germany, Japan)
Semi-presidential system: both a powerful President and a PM (France, Russia, Sri Lanka)
Comparison table of executive types across countries
Why India chose the parliamentary system: experience under British rule, accountability, avoiding personality cult

sections.name: 4.3 Parliamentary Executive in India: Power and Position of the President

concepts.text: President as nominal head; real power with PM-led Council of Ministers
Indirect election of the President by an electoral college of MPs and MLAs using STV
Term of five years; removal by impeachment for violation of the Constitution
Formal powers: executive, legislative, financial, military and diplomatic, exercised on ministers' advice
Article 74(1): President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers; can return advice once for reconsideration
Right to be informed of important matters and decisions
Sending back bills (except money bills) and advice for reconsideration; 'pocket veto'
Choosing the Prime Minister when no party or coalition has a clear majority
Vice-President: election, ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha, acts as President when vacant

sections.name: 4.5 Prime Minister and Council of Ministers

concepts.text: PM must command majority support in Lok Sabha; non-members must be elected within six months
PM chooses ministers and allocates portfolios; Council of Ministers capped at 15% of Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003)
Collective responsibility to Lok Sabha; government falls on a vote of no confidence
Cabinet ministers, ministers of state, deputy ministers
Influence of coalition politics on the PM's power
State executive: Governor (appointed) and Chief Minister with council of ministers
Bureaucracy as trained civil servants who advise ministers and implement policies
Political neutrality and permanence of civil servants
All India Services (IAS, IPS), central and state services; UPSC and state PSCs recruit
Reservations in recruitment for SC, ST and OBC
Criticism: red tape, insensitivity, political interference; RTI as a check
Exercise type: distinguish nominal and real executive; explain types of executive with examples

sections.name: 5.1 Why do we need a Parliament?

concepts.text: Legislature as the central forum of representative democracy: law-making, debate, accountability
Parliament also elects/removes officials, represents diverse views, controls finances
Decline of legislatures relative to executive dominance

sections.name: 5.2 Why do we need two Houses of Parliament?

concepts.text: Bicameral vs unicameral legislatures; states with Legislative Councils
Rajya Sabha: represents States, indirectly elected by MLAs, permanent house, one-third retire every two years
Unequal representation of States in Rajya Sabha (based on population) vs equal (USA Senate)
12 nominated members of Rajya Sabha from literature, science, art and social service
Lok Sabha: directly elected, territorial constituencies, five-year term, can be dissolved earlier
Functions: legislative, control of executive, financial, representative, debating, constituent, electoral, judicial (impeachment)
Powers of Lok Sabha: money bills, budget, no-confidence motion
Powers of Rajya Sabha: delays non-money bills, recommends on money bills within 14 days
Special powers of Rajya Sabha: Article 249 (State list subjects in national interest), All-India services

sections.name: 5.4 How does the Parliament make laws?

concepts.text: Stages of a bill: drafting, first reading, committee, second reading, third reading
Government bills vs private members' bills; money bills vs non-money bills
Passage in the other House; joint sitting of both Houses to resolve deadlock
President's assent completes law-making
Flowchart activity: trace a bill from introduction to Act

sections.name: 5.5 How does the Parliament control the executive?

concepts.text: Deliberation and discussion: Question Hour, Zero Hour, adjournment motion, calling attention
Approval and ratification of laws
Financial control: budget approval, CAG reports, Public Accounts Committee
No-confidence motion as the ultimate check
Limits on control under strong majorities and party discipline

sections.name: 5.6 What do the Committees of Parliament do?

concepts.text: Standing committees (departmental) and ad hoc committees
Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPC) for investigations
Committees scrutinise bills, demands for grants and government functioning in detail

sections.name: 5.7 How does the Parliament regulate itself?

concepts.text: Presiding officer (Speaker/Chairman) as final authority on house conduct
Anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985; 91st Amendment, 2003): disqualification for defection
Parliamentary privileges
Exercise type: compare powers of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; explain ways of executive control

sections.name: 6.1 Why do we need an Independent Judiciary?

concepts.text: Judiciary settles disputes, protects rights and upholds the rule of law
Independence: other organs must not interfere; judges decide without fear or favour
Independence does not mean arbitrariness; judiciary is accountable to the Constitution
Legislature not involved in appointment of judges
Fixed tenure, retirement age and difficult removal procedure
Salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, not voted by legislature
Actions and decisions of judges cannot be criticised personally; power to punish contempt
Chief Justice of India appointed (convention of seniority), with controversy over supersessions
Collegium system: CJI and senior-most judges recommend appointments
Role of the executive in formal appointment; debate on executive vs judicial primacy
Removal only for proven misbehaviour or incapacity
Motion with special majority in both Houses of Parliament
Rare use: e.g. the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami failed
Single integrated judicial system: Supreme Court, High Courts, District and subordinate courts
Functions of each level in the hierarchy
Decisions of the Supreme Court binding on all courts
Original jurisdiction: Centre-State and inter-State disputes
Writ jurisdiction: protect fundamental rights (Art. 32); High Courts under Art. 226
Appellate jurisdiction: highest court of appeal in civil, criminal and constitutional cases
Advisory jurisdiction: President can seek opinion (Art. 143); advice not binding
Special powers: special leave to appeal (Art. 136) and complete justice (Art. 142)
Public Interest Litigation (PIL): relaxed locus standi, petitions by third parties or letters
Origins in the late 1970s-80s (e.g. Hussainara Khatoon, bonded labour, prisoners' rights)
Positive effects: access to justice for poor, accountability of executive
Criticism: overburdening courts, blurring separation of powers

sections.name: 6.8 Judiciary and Rights; Judiciary and Parliament

concepts.text: Judicial review: power to declare laws unconstitutional
Protection of rights via writs and judicial review
Conflicts with Parliament over property right and amendment power: Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Basic structure doctrine as limit on Parliament
Issues of privileges and contempt between legislature and judiciary
Exercise type: identify jurisdiction used in given cases; arguments for/against judicial activism
Federalism: two or more levels of government with constitutionally divided powers
Key features: dual government, written constitution, division of powers, independent judiciary to settle disputes
Examples of strain: break-up of the Soviet Union, the West Indies Federation, Nigeria
Federalism suits diverse societies but needs a federal spirit, not just structures
Constitution calls India a 'Union of States' rather than a federation
Division of powers through Seventh Schedule: Union List, State List, Concurrent List
Residuary powers with the Union
Examples of subjects in each list (defence, police, education etc.)

sections.name: 7.3 Federalism with a Strong Central Government

concepts.text: Reasons for strong Centre: Partition, integration of states, development needs
Parliament can alter boundaries and names of states (Art. 3)
Emergency provisions make the system unitary
Financial dependence of states on Centre; Finance Commission and grants
Governor's role, All-India services and Centre's power over State bills
Centre-State relations: shift from Congress dominance to coalition and assertive state parties
Demands for autonomy: more powers, financial autonomy, administrative, cultural/linguistic
Role of Governors and President's Rule (Art. 356); misuse and S.R. Bommai judgement
Sarkaria Commission (1983) recommendations on Governors
Demands for new states: linguistic reorganisation; Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand (2000), Telangana (2014)
Interstate conflicts: border disputes (Belgaum, Chandigarh) and river water disputes (Cauvery, Narmada)
Asymmetric federalism: special provisions for certain states (Art. 371 for North-East and others)
Special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and its abrogation in 2019
Reorganisation of J&K into two Union Territories (J&K and Ladakh)
Exercise type: classify subjects into lists; explain conflicts and their resolution mechanisms
Local government as government at village and district/town level closest to people
Benefits: participation, local knowledge, efficiency, democratic decentralisation
Case example of a village dispute settled locally (activity type)

sections.name: 8.2 Growth of Local Government in India

concepts.text: Ancient sabhas and village panchayats; Lord Ripon's local self-government (1882)
Gandhi's vision of gram swaraj; Directive Principle (Art. 40) on village panchayats
Community Development Programme (1952); Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) three-tier recommendation
Weakness of early local bodies: lack of funds, irregular elections, state control
Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) and L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) push for constitutional status
73rd Amendment (1992) for rural local bodies; 74th Amendment for urban local bodies; in force 1993
Three-tier structure: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti (block), Zila Parishad (district)
Gram Sabha: all adult voters of a village
Direct elections every five years; fresh elections within six months if dissolved
Reservations: one-third seats and chairperson posts for women; SC/ST seats in proportion to population; option for OBCs
Transfer of 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule
State Election Commission conducts panchayat elections
State Finance Commission reviews finances of local bodies every five years
74th Amendment: municipal corporations, municipalities, nagar panchayats; 18 subjects in Twelfth Schedule
PESA Act 1996 extends panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas with tribal customs
Regular elections and huge numbers of elected representatives including women and SC/ST
Problems: limited funds, dependence on state and central grants, little real devolution
Growth of women's participation and leadership
Exercise type: identify tiers and features; evaluate implementation of the amendments

chapters.title: Constitution: Constitution as a Living Document

concepts.text: Constitutions must be adaptable to changing circumstances while preserving core values
Indian Constitution has worked for over seven decades with many amendments
Comparison with countries that replaced constitutions frequently
Article 368 lays out amendment procedure
Amendment by simple majority (outside Art. 368, e.g. creating states)
Special majority: majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting in each House
Special majority plus ratification by half of state legislatures for federal provisions
No referendum or special body; Parliament initiates; both Houses must pass separately
Balance of rigidity and flexibility in the amendment process

sections.name: 9.3 Why have there been so many amendments?

concepts.text: Contents of amendments: technical/administrative changes (e.g. retirement age, salaries)
Differing interpretations of the Constitution between judiciary and government
Amendments through political consensus (e.g. 52nd anti-defection, 61st voting age 18, 73rd/74th)
Amendments of the 1970s: 38th, 39th and 42nd during the Emergency
42nd Amendment (1976): wide changes, Preamble words, curbs on judicial review
44th Amendment (1978) reversed many 42nd Amendment changes

sections.name: 9.5 Basic Structure and Evolution of the Constitution

concepts.text: Golaknath case (1967): Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): Parliament can amend but not alter the basic structure
Elements of basic structure: supremacy of Constitution, secularism, federalism, judicial review, etc.
Basic structure doctrine as judicial contribution to constitutional evolution
Contribution of the judiciary: expanding meanings (e.g. Art. 21), limits on reservations (50%)
Maturity of political leadership in accepting judicial verdicts
Exercise type: classify amendments by type; explain basic structure doctrine with cases

chapters.title: Constitution: The Philosophy of the Constitution

sections.name: 10.1 What is meant by Philosophy of the Constitution?

concepts.text: Constitution's philosophy: the moral and political values underlying its provisions
Studying concepts like rights, citizenship, democracy and their interpretation

sections.name: 10.2 Constitution as Means of Democratic Transformation

concepts.text: Constitution limits state power and also enables peaceful social change
Using constitutional means to break caste hierarchy and colonial legacy

sections.name: 10.3 Why do we need to go back to the Constituent Assembly?

concepts.text: Constituent Assembly Debates as a source to understand intentions behind provisions
Assembly debates reveal reasons, alternatives considered and compromises

sections.name: 10.4 What is the Political Philosophy of our Constitution?

concepts.text: Commitment to individual freedom (freedom of expression, against arbitrary arrest)
Social justice: reservations for SC/ST/OBC, compensatory discrimination
Respect for diversity and minority rights: community-sensitive approach
Secularism: no official religion, principled distance between state and religion
Freedom of religion of individuals and communities; state's right to intervene for reform
Universal franchise from the start, reflecting faith in people
Federalism with asymmetry, recognising regional and linguistic diversity
National identity that accommodates multiple identities
Faith in political deliberation and debate
Spirit of accommodation and compromise in the Assembly
Decision-making by consensus rather than majority voting
Criticism: unwieldy and very long
Criticism: not fully representative (indirectly elected Assembly)
Criticism: alien document borrowed from others
Responses to each criticism
Centralised idea of national unity
Gender-justice issues, especially within the family, left unresolved
Some socio-economic rights put in DPSP rather than FR
Exercise type: link provisions to underlying values; evaluate criticisms

chapters.title: Political Theory: Political Theory: An Introduction

concepts.text: Common negative views of politics (dirty tricks, self-interest)
Politics as the process of collective decision-making and pursuit of a good society
Politics involves negotiation, decisions by governments and people's movements

sections.name: 11.2 What do we study in Political Theory?

concepts.text: Political theory examines ideas such as freedom, equality, justice, democracy, secularism
Clarifying meanings of concepts and examining how they are applied
Ideas of thinkers: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Marx, Gandhi, Ambedkar
Rousseau on freedom as the essence of humanity; Marx on equality; Gandhi on swaraj; Ambedkar on social justice
Applying concepts to issues: e.g. what equality means in reservations or opportunities
Political theory tests beliefs through reasoned argument
Activity type: debate on whether certain policies are fair

sections.name: 11.4 Why should we study Political Theory?

concepts.text: Useful for everyone: politicians, bureaucrats, lawyers, activists and citizens
Helps develop informed opinions and reasoning on public issues
Encourages tolerance and examining one's own prejudices
Exercise type: identify which concept is at stake in given situations
Freedom as a central political ideal; struggles for freedom (e.g. Nelson Mandela's Long Walk to Freedom)
Aung San Suu Kyi's 'Freedom from Fear' as an example
Freedom as absence of external constraints
Freedom also as the expansion of conditions for self-development
Swaraj: self-rule over oneself and society; Gandhi's Hind Swaraj
Sources of constraints: domination, external control, social inequality, economic inequality
Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's idea of freedom
Some constraints are needed to prevent harm and live together peacefully
Distinction between justified and unjustified constraints
Liberalism: emphasis on individual liberty and toleration
J.S. Mill's harm principle: society can restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others
Self-regarding vs other-regarding actions
Minor harm deserves social disapproval; serious harm justifies legal restriction
Negative liberty: area of non-interference where the individual is free from external constraint
Positive liberty: freedom to develop oneself, requiring enabling conditions (education, health)
Isaiah Berlin's distinction between the two concepts
Freedom of expression as part of the minimum area of non-interference
Banning books and films: debates on censorship (e.g. Satanic Verses, Deepa Mehta's Water)
Reasonable restrictions on freedom; constraints we accept voluntarily vs imposed
Activity type: debate on dress codes and other social restrictions
Exercise type: distinguish negative and positive liberty; evaluate reasonable restrictions
Equality as a powerful moral and political ideal; equal worth of all humans
Coexistence of global inequalities in wealth and opportunity
Equality of opportunity: everyone should have equal chances to develop talents
Natural inequalities (abilities, talents) vs social inequalities (created by society)
Social inequalities are unjust and should be corrected
Political equality: equal citizenship, voting rights, civil liberties
Social equality: equal life chances, access to education, health, ending caste and gender discrimination
Economic equality: reducing gaps in wealth and income
Feminism: equal rights for women and men; patriarchy as a social, not natural, system
Socialism: reducing inequality through state action, public control of key resources; Ram Manohar Lohia's five inequalities
Establishing formal equality: removing legal privileges and discrimination
Equality through differential treatment: special help for disadvantaged groups
Affirmative action: reservations and other measures to correct historic inequalities
Debate on reservations as a means to achieve social equality
Exercise type: classify cases as natural or social inequality; evaluate differential treatment
Justice in different traditions: dharma, Confucius, Plato's Republic
Kant: human dignity and treating each person as an end
Equal treatment for equals: same rights for all regardless of caste, gender etc.
Proportionate justice: rewards in proportion to effort and skill
Recognition of special needs: extra help for disabled and disadvantaged
Social justice involves fair distribution of goods, opportunities and services
Land reforms, reservations and other measures of redistribution in India
Debate on special treatment vs equal opportunity
Rawls' veil of ignorance: choose rules without knowing your position in society
Rational people would choose rules protecting the worst-off
Fair rules as the basis of a just society
Ensuring minimum basic needs: food, health, housing, education, minimum wages
Government programmes for the poor; poverty and inequality in India
Free markets vs state intervention: arguments of free-market supporters
Arguments for state intervention: markets ignore the disadvantaged
Exercise type: apply the three principles of justice to scenarios; explain the veil of ignorance
Right as a justified claim recognised by society and the state
Rights are claims necessary for a life of dignity and well-being
Not every desire or want is a right
Natural rights theory: rights given by nature/God (life, liberty, property)
Human rights: all persons are entitled to certain rights by virtue of being human
Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and expanding claims of rights
Rights are recognised and protected through laws and constitutions
Rights limit the state and also require state action
Political rights: vote, contest elections, form parties
Civil liberties: fair trial, expression, protest
Economic rights: basic needs, work, minimum wage
Cultural rights: mother-tongue education, preserving language and culture
Rights entail obligations of the state and duties of citizens
Respecting others' rights; balancing conflicting rights
Debates: security vs civil liberties (e.g. surveillance, preventive detention)
Exercise type: classify rights; explain the link between rights and responsibilities
Citizenship as full and equal membership of a political community
Citizenship is a status with rights and obligations
Rights of movement, residence and work across the country
Migrants and debates over 'outsiders' in cities
Struggles for citizenship rights (e.g. US civil rights movement)
Equal rights for the urban poor and marginalised such as slum dwellers and tribal peoples
Equal citizenship requires policies addressing different needs
T.H. Marshall's civil, political and social rights
Nation-states define criteria for citizenship (birth, descent, naturalisation)
Indian citizenship law and the Constitution's inclusive conception
Problem of stateless persons and refugees
Ideal of universal citizenship within a state vs exclusionary practices
Global citizenship: shared humanity across borders
Global problems (e.g. environment, disasters) need cross-border solidarity
Exercise type: explain full and equal membership; debate global citizenship
Nationalism's role in uniting peoples and in breaking empires
Nationalism as both a unifying and divisive force
A nation is an 'imagined community' based on collective beliefs and aspirations
Shared beliefs: nations exist because members believe in them
History: a sense of continuing historical identity
Territory: attachment to a homeland
Shared political ideals: democracy, liberal values
Common political identity rather than single religion or language
Claim of nations to govern themselves and have their own state
Problems: one culture-one state leads to creating minorities and conflict
Need to accommodate minorities within states
Recognising rights of minorities: language, culture, religion
Indian approach of accommodating diverse groups
Rabindranath Tagore's critique of narrow nationalism
Exercise type: identify features of a nation; discuss national self-determination
Secularism as opposition to religious domination
Inter-religious domination: one religious community dominating another
Intra-religious domination: domination within a religion (caste, gender)
Secularism as a normative doctrine for a society free from both dominations
Separation of religious institutions and state institutions
State not run by religious leaders or based on one religion
Secular state must promote peace, freedom and equality
Mutual exclusion of state and religion (US/French model)
Focus on individual rights; little concern for community rights
Indian secularism addresses both inter- and intra-religious domination
Principled distance: state may engage with religion to promote equality
Support for minority institutions and state-led reforms (e.g. temple entry, untouchability abolition)
Anti-religious: alleged threat to religious identity
Western import: seen as alien to Indian culture
